title: Your Handy 1996–2002 BMW Z3 Buyer’s Guide
summary: The early 1990s brought a virtual Cambrian Explosion of life to the affordable roadster segment. body_markdown:
The early 1990s brought a virtual Cambrian Explosion of life to the affordable roadster segment. There was the[Mazda Miata](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mazda/mx~5_miata/1991/1991-mazda-mx~5_miata-base?id=aCn1I000000DREPSA4) , of course, but the Germans also brought out the[Porsche Boxster](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/boxster/1997/1997-porsche-boxster-base?id=aCn1I000000CxH4SAK) ,[Mercedes-Benz SLK](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=mercedes-benz+slk) , and BMW Z3. All had their own set of virtues and vices, but only one remains in production, affordable, and relevant today. For an entirely new generation of enthusiasts, the answer is always Miata. Prices of prime examples of early NA (1990–97) Miatas reflect this. Not ideal for those who must have the Mazda, but bargain hunters can rejoice at the often overlooked BMW Z3. In several ways it was the better car, and today values aren’t too far apart even though the BMW was the far pricier choice in the ‘90s.


The Z3 hewed closely to the old British sports car formula, not just in layout but also in the strategy of borrowing heavily from the parts bin of existing cars. Rather than using BMW’s more modern E36/E46 multi link rear suspension, the Z3 borrowed the semi-trailing arm setup from the older[E30](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/bmw/318i/1991/1991-bmw-318i-base?id=aCn1I000000DG3pSAG) compact. This allowed BMW to keep the cost down, and was in line with the car’s mission to evoke the vintage feel of classic roadsters. It also, conveniently, freed up space for a larger fuel tank and a space-saver spare.


BMW


The Z3 also had the distinction of being one of the first BMWs assembled in its new Spartanburg, South Carolina plant. The specs of the initial car were modest and, ah-hem, a bit Miata-like. The nearly $30,000 price (compared to under $19K for the Miata), however, wasn’t. The 1.9-liter DOHC four-cylinder managed just under 140 horsepower, and there was a 200-pound weight penalty compared with the Mazda, with the Z3 weighing about 2600 pounds despite being only about 3 inches longer.


Road testers nevertheless loved the Z3. In its 1996 test, *Car and Driver* called the four-cylinder Z3 “eager rather than fast,” but also noted that BMW’s smooth controls “give the driver a great feeling of harmony with the machinery.” Further praise came in for the clutch, light power steering, and the car’s propensity to understeer predictably under power then flick its tail out when the driver lifts off the throttle. Overall, the magazine likened the early Z3 to a slightly grown up Miata.


BMW


Everyone who looked at the engine compartment realized there was room for more than the 1.9, but the initial cars were all four-cylinders with either a five-speed manual or a ZF automatic. Tops were mostly manual, but a power top and a neat removable hardtop came soon after the intro which took place at the January 1996 North American International Auto Show in Detroit, although the new James Bond, Pierce Bronson drove one in the 1995 film *Goldeneye.* 007 Edition cars in special Atlanta Blue Metallic and Tan were later sold to the public with special floor mats and a dash plaque.


The 1997 model year saw the addition of standard ASC (traction control) and the optional 190-hp, 2.8-liter straight-six that everyone expected from the beginning. Visually, the six was only distinguished by badging and a slightly wider rear track. Things got rapidly more interesting from there.


Sam Smith


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


[Julie Gu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/jguhagerty-com/)


The 1998 model year would be the last year of the 1.9-liter in North America and a limited-slip differential became standard on the sixes, but the big news was the introduction of the wide-body M Coupe and M Roadster, with distinctive rollover hoops that spread to the rest of the Z3 Roadsters. The Z3 M cars were powered by the 240-horsepower S52 engine from the E36 M3. Unlike the E36 M3, though, the only gearbox available on the Z3 M was a five-speed manual.


The Coupe body-style was a curiosity (which was subsequently offered in standard as well as the M version), and may be the quirkiest BMW since the[Isetta](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=bmw+isetta) . Rather than a fastback roofline, it was a long-roof with a Kamm-like tail. Basically, a tiny shooting brake. There are no rear seats, so headroom wasn’t a factor in the decision, and it makes for a reasonably practical little car that has gained a massive cult following and the nickname “clown shoe.” Well-known automotive photographer Michael Alan Ross daily drives one with 240,000 miles on it. Its ability to accommodate his photography gear is legendary.


BMW


BMW


The 1999 model year was a significant one for the Z3, as the base engine was a 170-hp, 2.5-liter inline six (curiously badged as a 2.3). The 2.8-liter now made 193 hp, with the 3.2-liter M version still at 240 hp. There was also a modest facelift for 1999 (LCI or Life Cycle Impulse in BMW-speak). The wider rear-track that had been 2.8 and M exclusive was standardized, along with updated lighting, (new headlamps and taillamps and a smoother rear third brake light). Inside, there was a new center console and a better-looking steering wheel and a better insulated top, although still with a plastic rear window. Mechanically, there was a more advanced traction control (DSC) and BMW’s solenoid-operated variable valve timing system (VANOS) made for a fatter torque curve.


Calendar year 2000 (MY 2001) saw BMW shift engine families from M52 to M54 and the cars became a little less analog, now with both DSC and an electronic throttle. The base 2.5-liter six-cylinder engine had 184 hp, the 3.0-liter midrange engine offered 225 hp, nearly matching the previous M, and the S54 3.2-liter M motor now made a massive 315 hp. *Car and Driver* confessed that the car “simply makes you do bad things,” like 0-60 in 4.8 seconds. True, the car’s ethos had changed along with its weight (up about 400 pounds from the original 1.9 Z3) and price (up to about $48,000), but it all seemed in line with what you got. The Z3 wound down in 2002 as Spartanburg got ready to gear up for the Chris Bangle-designed Z4.


Sandon Voelker


## What to Look for


The oldest Z3s are now 30 years old. On cars that have seen regular use, nearly everything that can wear out is worn out by now. One of my co-workers has used a 1.9 Z3 as a commuter car for at least five years. With over 230,000 miles, it’s a textbook example of what a high-mileage Z3 is like. Mechanically, nearly every bushing has been replaced twice. The cooling system, (a classic BMW weak point), has also been largely gone over twice—plastic radiators and plastic coolant reservoirs are 100K mile replacement items, along with hoses and water pumps. Early cars using the analog mechanical throttle can also be sidelined by a $4 throttle cable bushing. The 1.9-liter twin-cam four, however, has proven stout. It remains quiet and peppy, with little appetite for oil.


On VANOS equipped cars, 100K miles marks a major service which can include O-rings, seals, gaskets, anti-rattle components, (which produce a marbles in a dryer noise when they fail), and VANOS solenoids. Valve cover gaskets and pan gaskets tend to leak.


Another thing to inspect before buying: welds in the trunk. Spot welds can come apart where the rear differential mount attaches to the trunk floor, which over time can cause complete structural failure. Make sure to remove the trunk carpet and evaluate the condition of the welds. Separation can happen in any Z3 model, but higher-power cars—Ms especially—that tend to be driven harder are worth extra scrutiny. Repair and reinforcement kits are available, but labor is extensive and thus expensive.


Sandon Voelker


Eric Weiner


Eric Weiner


Sandon Voelker


Sandon Voelker


With good maintenance, all of the engines are robust, although high-mileage cars with casual maintenance can experience timing chain issues later in life. Automatic transmissions that don’t receive a fluid and filter change every 100,000 miles or so can be dicey. Changing the gearbox fluid every 40,000 to 50,000 miles on the 5-speed cars is a good idea, too. Gearbox wear presents with noise and failing synchromesh.


Interiors, especially on high-mileage roadsters that have seen lots of UV rays can be genuinely scary with warped and cracked plastic everywhere and sticky buttons. Napa leather seats wear poorly with many cars today displaying cracks and tears, or bad re-dye jobs. Weatherstripping and gaskets dry out and crumble, particularly on the antenna grommet, A-pillar, and taillight lenses. Door handles tend to rip off, and the plastic bushings in the seat rails wear out.


Happily, the bodywork is less of an issue. Z3s seldom rust badly, but clear coats fail and peel and headlights yellow with age. Tops are expensive to replace, with the later, fully lined items being the priciest. Because of space issues and the way the top folds, it’s impossible to fit a glass rear window, so yellowed and cracked plastic rear windows are a fact of life with Z3s that still wear their original tops.


## What to Pay


Predictably, the 1.9-liter cars are the bottom of the rung in terms of collectibility. They’re by no means bad cars, and they can be easy to live with, often with simple, manual tops and good fuel economy. Since the sixes are generally what people want, you can pick up a real bargain on a 1.9, typically in the mid- to high-four-figure range, roughly the space that NA Miatas occupied pre-COVID. Condition #3 (good) values in the Hagerty Price Guide are currently $8600 for 1.9-liter Z3s, and condition #2 (excellent) values only stretch to $13,800. Black, silver and red tend to be among the most common Z3 colors, and the market will certainly pay up for unusual colors and special interiors.


Six-cylinder, non-M cars in driver condition start at around $10,000 or so for #3 condition cars, while the condition #2 value for a for a later Z3 3.0 stretches past 22 grand. Base (non-M) Z3 Coupes, which came exclusively with the 2.8- or 3.0-liter engines, are rare and tend to bring roughly 50% more than equivalent Roadsters. The M cars, meanwhile, are really four markets: S52 Roadsters, S52 Coupes, S54 Roadsters, and S54 Coupes. S52 Coupes generally bring between $32,000 (condition #3) and $60,000 (condition #2). S54s run in the $50,000 range for condition #3 cars, while low-mile examples are capable of commanding six figures. M Roadsters are a relative bargain, with S52s in the $20,000 to $30,000 range and S54s in the $26,000 to $43,000 range.


BMW/Daniel Kraus


M cars, particularly the M Coupes, have been on an upward value trajectory for a while, but the base cars have been more steady. After some notable growth in the early 2020s, Z3 prices have been largely steady over the past few years. As for who’s buying Z3s, the core audience is surprisingly older than one might think given the BMW brand in general and the build date for these chuckable two-seaters. Nearly half of buyer interest, as measured by Hagerty insurance quote activity, comes from baby boomer enthusiasts, who only make up 34% of the collector car market as a whole. Younger buyers appear to have set their sights on the M badge, as millennials quote 34% of Z3 M cars despite only making up 21% of the market as a whole.


No matter how you dissect the Z3 market, though, there’s a lot of fun to be had for not a lot of money. And, in most cases, the dreaded BMW tax in maintenance really isn’t that bruising.


Sandon Voelker
